opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few fundamental reasons, and the most important one is data.

Language models are trained on text, and text is already a highly compressed, highly abstract representation of human knowledge. When people write something down, they've already done a lot of the thinking: they've picked out what matters, organized it, and expressed it in symbols that carry dense meaning. So next-token prediction on internet-scale text turns out to be an incredibly efficient way to absorb reasoning, common sense, and world knowledge.

Vision is very different. Pixels are raw signals from the physical world. They're high-dimensional, highly redundant, and most of what's in an image is irrelevant to whatever task you care about. Images are not the product of human abstraction the way language is. So the self-supervised objectives we have for vision, like reconstructing masked patches, predicting the next frame, or contrastive learning, haven't produced the kind of emergent intelligence that next-token prediction gave us in language. We haven't found vision's equivalent of "predict the next word."

Second, a lot of today's vision-language models are really language models with eyes attached. The vision encoder is often trained separately, for example with CLIP-style image-text alignment, and then plugged into an LLM. The alignment data is image-caption pairs, and captions describe only a tiny fraction of what's in an image, usually the salient objects. Fine-grained spatial relationships, 3D geometry, physical properties, how things would move if you pushed them: none of that is well captured. So these models can tell you "there's a cup on the table," but they're weak at precise localization, counting, spatial reasoning, and understanding what's physically possible.

Third, and this is the perspective I come from as someone working on embodied intelligence, I think true visual understanding is inseparable from action. Humans and animals don't learn to see by passively looking at billions of photos. We learn by interacting: reaching, grasping, moving around, seeing the consequences of our actions. Vision evolved to serve action. Today's models learn from static internet images and videos with no closed loop, no feedback from the physical world. They're missing that whole dimension of grounding.

So my view is that the next breakthrough in vision may not come from scaling up image-text pairs. It may come from combining vision with 3D understanding, physical simulation, and especially large amounts of embodied interaction data, where vision, language, and action are learned together. That's why I think embodied AI isn't just an application of vision-language models. It may be the path that pushes vision itself forward.

r001.rationale: It describes internet-scale text as a dense representation of knowledge, but does not say it covers a large proportion of the language humans might produce.

r002.rationale: It calls data the most important factor, but focuses on the nature of visual data, training objectives, and lack of embodied interaction rather than stating that insufficient training data is the fundamental reason.

r003.rationale: It notes that models can identify salient objects but are weak at several visual tasks; it does not contrast claims that they can do everything with how well they actually perform.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that we never gave vision its own "internet moment." Language models got lucky in a specific way: human beings had already spent twenty years writing down essentially everything they know as text, in a format that is naturally sequential, naturally compressed, and already carries the structure of reasoning inside it. A sentence is a trajectory of thought. When you train on trillions of tokens of that, you are not just learning pixels of words, you are absorbing how people argue, plan, and abstract. Vision has no equivalent corpus. We have billions of images, but an image is not a thought. It is raw sensor data, extremely redundant, and almost nothing about why the picture matters is contained in the picture itself.

So what did the field do? We took the language model, which already had the reasoning, and bolted a vision encoder onto the front of it. CLIP-style encoders, a projector, some captioning data, and suddenly the model can describe an image. That felt like a breakthrough, and in a sense it was. But look at what the model actually learned. It learned to translate an image into a handful of tokens that look like a caption, and then let the language model do everything else. The visual representation is a bottleneck, usually a few hundred tokens, and most of the fine-grained spatial and physical information is thrown away before reasoning even begins. That is why these models still fail at counting objects, reading a clock, judging whether one thing is behind another, or understanding what will happen if you push a cup toward the edge of a table. Those are not language problems. They are perception problems, and we outsourced perception to a frozen encoder trained to match captions.

The second issue is the objective. Next-token prediction on text is a wonderful self-supervised signal because text is already a model of the world written by intelligent agents. Predicting the next pixel or the next patch, by contrast, forces you to waste capacity on texture and noise that carries almost no semantic value. The community has tried contrastive learning, masked image modeling, joint-embedding approaches, and each of them captures part of the picture, but we do not yet have a visual pretraining target with the same beautiful alignment between what is easy to predict and what is worth knowing.

The third thing, and this is where my own work pushes me, is that vision ultimately is not about looking, it is about acting. We humans do not learn vision by staring at photographs with captions. We learn it by moving, grasping, failing, and seeing the consequence. Depth, occlusion, object permanence, affordance, all of that comes from embodiment. A vision-language model trained on static web images has never experienced a single consequence of a single action. So its "understanding" of the physical world is borrowed entirely from text descriptions written by people who did have bodies. That borrowed understanding is shallow in exactly the places robots need it to be deep.

So when people ask why VLMs lag behind LLMs, I would say the gap is not a matter of scale or a few more years of the same recipe. The language side has a data source, an objective, and an evaluation culture that fit together. The vision side is still running on borrowed infrastructure. Closing the gap probably means native multimodal pretraining where vision is not an attachment, much richer and more structured visual supervision, including video and 3D, and, I would argue, closing the loop with action so that the model has some way to ground what it sees in what happens next. Until then, we will keep getting systems that sound like they understand an image, because the language model is very good at sounding like it understands, while actually seeing far less than we assume.

r001.rationale: It says people have written down “essentially everything they know as text,” conveying that text covers a very large share of human expression and knowledge.

r002.rationale: It identifies the lack of an equivalent visual corpus as one reason, but presents several other causes and does not identify insufficient training data as the fundamental reason.

r003.rationale: It contrasts image description with failures on specific visual tasks, but does not address claims that current models can do everything.

astra-6.text:
I think a big part of the gap comes from the training signal. Language models learn from text that already contains a huge amount of human interpretation: people describe what happened, explain why it happened, and spell out relationships between ideas. So predicting the next token can teach a model much more than just how to construct sentences.

With vision, the input contains enormous amounts of information, but the supervision often captures only a small fraction of it. A caption might say, “A person is holding a cup.” It usually doesn’t explain how the fingers contact the cup, whether the grip is stable, or what would happen if the person tilted it. Those details matter for understanding the physical world, but a model can do well on image-text training without learning them.

And when we connect a vision encoder to a strong language model, the language model can sometimes compensate for weak visual understanding. It produces a plausible answer based on what typically happens, even if it hasn’t actually resolved the relevant detail in the image. Fluency can make that gap difficult to notice.

So I wouldn’t say the problem is simply that we need more images. We also need training objectives and data that make precise visual understanding necessary—potentially through video, interaction, and observing the consequences of actions. The question is how to give these models a learning signal for the visual world that is as rich and scalable as next-token prediction has been for language.

r001.rationale: The response says language text contains extensive human interpretation, but does not state that internet text covers a large proportion of the language humans might produce.

r002.rationale: It attributes the gap to limited richness of visual supervision and training objectives, and explicitly says the problem is not simply needing more images. It does not identify insufficient training data as the fundamental reason.

r003.rationale: The response notes that a model may give a plausible answer without resolving a visual detail, but it does not distinguish claims that current models can do everything from whether they perform those tasks well.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one major reason is that language gives us a very convenient interface for learning. Text already compresses a lot of human knowledge into concepts and relationships. Images contain much more raw information, but it’s less obvious which parts matter. A model has to learn that structure as well as connect it to language.

The training signal is also different. With text, predicting the next token gives you a simple objective that you can apply at enormous scale. With vision and language, a caption describes only a small part of an image. It might say, “A person is sitting at a table,” but leave out the spatial relationships, the objects in the background, and what the person is doing with their hands. So even a large collection of image-caption pairs provides fairly incomplete supervision.

And many vision-language models inherit much of their reasoning ability from a language model. They can produce a convincing answer without necessarily grounding every detail in the image. That becomes particularly apparent when you ask about precise locations, counting, or physical relationships.

So I wouldn’t say it’s simply a question of making the models bigger. We also need better training signals and tasks that force the model to use visual evidence. Video and interaction could help, because they reveal how the world changes and what happens when you take an action.

r001.rationale: It says text compresses human knowledge, but does not state that internet text covers a large proportion of the language people might produce.

r002.rationale: It describes incomplete image-caption supervision and the need for better signals, but does not identify insufficient training data as the fundamental reason for the gap.

r003.rationale: It notes that models can give convincing answers without grounding every detail, but does not distinguish claims that they can do everything from how well they perform those tasks.
